Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Accurately identify cervical spine injuries via a physical examination and standard imaging
studies.
Recognize and classify upper cervical and subaxial spine injuries.
List indications for the surgical and nonsurgical management of cervical spine injuries.
Review the technical aspects of surgical management of specific cervical spine fracture
patterns.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The cervical spine can be divided into the upper and subaxial regions, both of which are
subject to unique injury mechanisms and patterns.

Management of upper cervical spine fractures is unique to the level and pattern of the
fracture.
Management of traumatic subaxial cervical spine injuries follows uniform treatment principles.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Cervical spine injuries can be divided into upper cervical spine injuries and subaxial
cervical spine injuries (Resources 1 and 2). The upper cervical spine (occiput through C2)
comprises the osseoligamentous complex of the craniocervical junction, which consists
of the occiput, atlas, and axis vertebrae. The junctional relationship of the upper cervical
spine and the cranium relies on ligamentous stability rather than bony stability. The
bony anatomy of C1 and C2 is unique compared with the repetitive anatomic
configuration of the subaxial spine (C3 through C7).
Treatment Overview

Treatment Overview
The goals of management for all cervical spine injuries includes protection of the neural
elements, stabilization of the spine, and maintenance of alignment until bony union
occurs. Without compromising these objectives, the duration of immobilization and the
number of levels included in a fusion procedure should be limited.
All cervical spine injuries expose patients to a substantial risk of neurologic injuries and
mortality.1,2 In addition, the extent of the injury is unknown until the patient has
undergone workup via an appropriate physical examination and imaging studies.
Therefore, all precautions to protect patients from subsequent injury should be
respected during the initial evaluation.
Nonsurgical treatment is indicated for patients with a stable injury and most commonly
involves the use of an external cervical orthosis. After a well-fitting hard collar or a halo

vest (less commonly utilized because of poor tolerance) is applied and upright imaging
studies confirm injury stability, the patient should be mobilized. Geriatric patients may
be at risk of aspiration while wearing a cervical orthosis; therefore, care must be taken to
monitor swallowing. The authors of this lesson suggest performing a swallow evaluation
to ensure that immobilization of the cervical spine of patients older than 65 years does
not increase their risk of aspiration.
Occipital Condyle Fractures
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Incidence: 3% to 16%
Occipital condyle fractures can occur in isolation or may be associated with occipitocervical
dissociation, which is associated with high spinal cord injuries.
The Anderson classification system is the most widely recognized classification system for
occipital condyle fractures.
The sensitivity of plain radiographs is low with regard to diagnosis; therefore, CT is mandatory
if the mechanism of trauma puts the patient at risk.
The Anderson and Montesano classification system is used to classify occipital condyle
fractures. The system categorizes fractures into three types (Figure 1).
Type I fractures are comminuted without displacement.
Type II injuries are skull-based fractures.
Type III fractures are avulsion injuries.
Figure 1 Illustrations show the classification of occipital condyle fractures. (Reproduced from
Anderson PA, Hah RJ: Occipitocervical and subaxial cervical trauma, in Truumees E, Prather H,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
3/40

eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 395-418.)

Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Appreciation of isolated occipital condyle fractures has increased because of the
increased use of CT in patients with spine trauma. Level IV evidence suggests that more
than one-half of patients with an occipital condyle fracture have an associated cervical
spine injury at a different level and 44% of patients with an occipital condyle fracture
have a potentially unstable fracture.3 Surgeons must be aware of this potential
association because it occurs in 1% to 3% of patients who sustain blunt craniocervical
trauma4 and is associated with a 20% mortality rate.5 If a more severe injury is present,
findings may include high cervical spine pain; torticollis; headaches (elevated intracranial
pressure); spinal cord injury; and cranial nerve IX, X, and XI palsies.6
Management
Factors to consider in comparing treatment options include stability of the occipitocervical
joint, presence and severity of other upper cervical spine injuries, and pattern of the occipital
condyle fracture.

Management
If using the Anderson classification system, a cervical orthosis, such as hard collar,
typically can be used to immobilize type I, II, and stable type III fractures. Occipitocervical
dissociation must be ruled out, particularly in patients with a type III fracture. Two
retrospective studies demonstrate moderate disability levels after nonsurgical
management.5,7

Unstable type III fractures with neural compression from fracture, chronic pain, or
associated occipitoatlantal or atlantoaxial injuries should be managed via
occipitocervical fusion.
Occipitocervical Dissociation
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Occipitocervical dissociations arise from compromise of the ligamentous restraints spanning
the craniocervical junction.
The craniocervical junction is maintained by the alar ligaments, the tectorial membrane, and
the alanto-occipital joint capsules; disruption of all three is required for craniocervical
dissociation.8
Occipitocervical injuries may be subtle and easily missed; however, these injuries may result in
severe neurologic consequences if they are not recognized and stabilized.
Several strategies to critically evaluate CT scans may help surgeons recognize these injuries.
Traynelis classification system
Type I: anterior displacement of the occiput on the atlas
Type II: longitudinal distraction
Type III: posterior subluxation or disassociation
Harborview classification
Stage 1: MRI evidence of injury to the craniocervical osseoligamentous stabilizers;
craniocervical alignment within 2 mm of normal; distraction of less than or equal to 2 mm on
provocative traction radiographs.
Stage 2: MRI evidence of injury to the craniocervical osseoligamentous stabilizers;
craniocervical alignment within 2 mm of normal; distraction of more than 2 mm on
provocative traction radiographs.
Stage 3: craniocervical malalignment of more than 2 mm on static radiographs.

Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Occipitocervical dissociation is associated with a high mortality rate. Recognizing this
injury is critical because failure to identify and stabilize it in a timely fashion is associated
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
5/40

with an increased risk of substantial neurologic deterioration.9 Approximately 25% of
these injuries are not initially identified.10 Proper evaluation begins with a patient history
and physical examination. This injury most commonly results from a high-energy
mechanism with associated head and/or facial trauma. The patient may have a
neurologic injury resulting in deficits within the extremities from spinal cord injury;
however, the injury may manifest as cranial nerve injury because of the proximity to the
brainstem. In addition, the incidence of vertebral artery injury is 10% to 50%; 20% of
patients with these injuries will have an associated stroke.9,11 If occipitocervical
dissociation is suspected, CT and/or MRI is recommended. Several methods can be used
for critical evaluation of CT scans if occipitocervical injuries are suspected.
The occipitocervical joints should be congruent on all CT scans. The occipital condyle-C1
interval is less than 1.5 mm. Measurements outside this range are consistent with
occipitocervical dissociation lesions.12
A level IV study of 59 patients occipitocervical dislocation suggested that several
commonly used techniques (Harris lines, 27.3% sensitivity; Powers ratio, 54.5%
sensitivity) were associated with poor sensitivity but 100% specificity.12
The classic Powers ratio lacks the sensitivity and specificity to be useful, partly because
the occipital condyle may lie anterior, posterior, or in a distracted position at any point in
time. In a patient with a straight distraction, the ratio would remain normal despite a
severe injury.
Harris lines include two measurements. One is a line drawn from the basion to the tip of
the odontoid. The second line is drawn by creating a line parallel to the posterior cortex
of the C2 body/odontoid and then drawing a line perpendicular from that line to the tip
of the odontoid. Both measurements should be less than 12 mm (Figure 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
6/40

Figure 2 Sagittal CT scan of the odontoid shows the Harris lines. One line is drawn from
the tip of the clivus (basion) to the tip of the odontoid. The second line is drawn by
creating a line parallel to the posterior cortex of the odontoid and then drawing a
perpendicular line from that line to the tip of the clivus. Both of those measurements
should be less than 12 mm in patients without occipitocervical dissociation. (Courtesy of
John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
If an occipitocervical injury is suspected but CT scans are inconclusive, MRI may help
identify areas of injury. Specifically, signs consistent with occipitocervical injuries include
increased fluid in the occipitocervical joints, elevation of the posterior longitudinal
ligament off clivus, or anterior soft-tissue swelling (Figure 3).
The Traynelis classification system is less frequently used because displacement may
vary with positioning.13 The Harborview classification system can be used to guide
treatment decisions.14

Figure 3 T2-weighted sagittal MRI of a cervical spine shows occipitocervical dissociation.
Distraction and effusion can be observed within the occiput-C1 joint with lack of joint
congruity. (Courtesy of John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
Management
Early stabilization of occipitocervical injury is paramount to protect the spinal cord before
definitive management.
Occipitocervical fusion is the most common definitive treatment option for occipitocervical
injuries; however, rare exceptions may be amenable to immobilization in an orthosis.

Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
8/40

If occipitocervical injuries are identified, strict immobilization must be maintained to
avoid neurologic injury. This immobilization involves a hard collar and often sandbags
placed on both sides of head with the use of tape to rigidly immobilize the head.15
Traction is absolutely contraindicated. Raising the head of the bed 30° may allow for a
gravity-assisted reduction of the occipitocervical joint. A poorly fitting cervical orthosis
may distract across the occipitocervical joint if it is too long. A lateral plain radiograph
should be obtained after the brace has been placed to ensure that the brace is not
causing excessive distraction of the occiput-C1 joint. A temporary halo vest may be
considered; however, care must be taken to avoid distraction.
The definitive treatment option is posterior occipitocervical fusion, most commonly from
the occiput to C2, depending on associated injuries. Extreme care should be taken to
fuse the neck in anatomic alignment in all directions to allow natural forward gaze and
prevent dysphagia from over-flexion or over-extension. A systematic review
demonstrated that this strategy may protect patients from neurologic decline; however,
nonsurgical management was successful in less than one-half of patients.15
Improvement in neurologic function is observed in approximately 20% of patients that
survive this injury.10 Although occipitocervical fusion is a more reliable treatment option,
it may result in substantial long-term implications for cervical motion. Approximately
50% of lateral rotation and flexion extension will be lost. Rare milder forms of
occipitocervical injury are amenable to management with the use of a hard collar and
can avoid the loss of cervical motion associated with successful occiput-C2 fusion. If
radiographic findings appears subtle or mild, a traction test can be performed to
determine if the injury is stable enough to be a candidate for nonsurgical
management.14 This test is performed in the operating room with the patient under
anesthesia, with a plan to proceed directly to posterior fusion if substantial motion is
observed at the occipitocervical joint. Gardner-Wells tongs are applied, and firm manual
longitudinal traction is applied under live fluoroscopic imaging. If no firm endpoint is
observed or if distraction across the occipital joint is greater than 2 mm, the injury is
considered unstable, and the patient should be treated via posterior fusion. If the injury
is stable, a cervical collar is used for 12 weeks, and the patient is monitored closely via
radiographs.

Atlas (C1) Fractures
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Neurologic injuries are uncommon in patients with a C1 ring fracture, and most of these
fractures can be managed with the use of a cervical orthosis.
Long-term prognosis depends on the integrity of the transverse ligament.
C1 fracture classification
Type 1: posterior arch fracture
Type 2: burst (Jefferson) fracture, involving the posterior and anterior arches
Type 3: anterior arch fracture
Type 4: lateral mass fracture
MRI is associated with increased sensitivity in detecting ligamentous disruption.
Type 1 injuries are midsubstance ruptures of the transverse ligament.
Type 2 injuries involve an avulsion of the ligament.19

Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
C1 ring injuries are more common in younger patient populations and are sustained
during higher energy mechanisms of injury. These injuries also result from low-energy
mechanisms in older patients with compromised bone quality. In 20% of patients, C1
fractures are associated with other upper cervical fractures or dislocations; therefore,
these fractures may be a sign of a more substantial injury that often will dictate
management.16 Neurologic injury is uncommon in patients with an isolated C1 ring
fracture because a substantial amount of room is available at this level for the spinal
cord. For example, in the classic Jefferson fracture, which involves bilateral fractures of
the anterior and posterior arches, the ring expands outward, away from the spinal cord.
Stability depends on the integrity of the transverse ligament.17 If the transverse ligament
is disrupted, the lateral mass of C1 can drift laterally off the articulation with the superior
facet of C2 if subjected to gravity. In its most severe form, this disruption may result in
the occipital condyle contacting the C2 facet, creating a cock-robin appearance if
unilateral or cranial settling if bilateral. Serial odontoid plain radiographs are the most
commonly cited imaging study for determining the integrity of the transverse ligament
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
10/40

and the propensity of the C1 lateral mass to displace. The lateral offset of the lateral
mass of C1 relative to the lateral mass of C2 is measured along the lateral border on the
left and right; these values are then added together, with a total of greater than 6.9 mm
indicating an unstable injury warranting surgical management. Although this
methodology is well recognized, a recent retrospective study demonstrated that only 9%
of patients with an MRI-confirmed transverse atlantal ligament injury had C1 lateral
mass overhang greater than 3 mm.18 MRIs can be used to directly visualize the
transverse ligament but must be obtained for this purpose, with fine cuts requested
through the area of interest; otherwise, this injury may be missed.
Management
Most C1 ring fractures are stable injuries and can be managed via immobilization in a cervical
orthosis.
The integrity of the transverse ligament is the main factor in deciding between nonsurgical and
surgical management.

Management
Most C1 ring injuries are stable and amenable to nonsurgical management; however,
some fractures are not stable and may require surgical management. Determining
whether surgical or nonsurgical management is necessary is not clearly defined in the
literature; however, some general guidelines can be followed. In addition, long-term
outcomes of patients with an isolated atlas fracture have been shown to be treatment-
independent.20
Isolated anterior and posterior arch fractures and transverse process atlas fractures, can
be managed nonsurgically via 6 to 12 weeks of external immobilization in a cervical
collar. In this situation, serial radiographs should be obtained and scrutinized for
displacement of the lateral masses. Burst fractures involving the anterior and posterior
arches with an intact transverse ligament (<7 mm of combined lateral overhang of lateral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
11/40

masses) are considered stable injuries and also can be managed via external
immobilization with the use of a halo vest or cervical collar.
Combined lateral mass displacement greater than 7 mm suggests injury to the
transverse ligament and an unstable injury. Identifying this type of injury is important
because loss of transverse atlantal ligament integrity may result in instability, regardless
of the ability of the C1 fracture to heal. A unilateral C1 lateral mass fracture does not
follow the 6.9-mm rule because only one lateral mass displaces (Figure 4). These
fractures may result in a cock-robin deformity and must be evaluated closely for
displacement that warrants surgical management.
Figure 4 Axial CT scan of a cervical spine shows a displaced unilateral C1 lateral mass
fracture. (Courtesy of John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
The goal of surgical management is to reestablish the C1 lateral mass in its proper
relationship to C2. Applying traction to the head often reduces the C1-2 joint. Historical
management included 6 weeks of traction followed by halo vest immobilization. The use
of C1-2 trans-articular screws is an option; however, posterior C1 lateral mass screws
and C2 pedicle screws (Harms technique) currently are more commonly used. In patients
with more severe injuries, particularly those with an associated injury, such as an
impaction fracture of the articular surface, spanning fusion from the occiput to C2 may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
12/40

be considered. All these treatment options involve fusing the upper cervical joint, which
results in substantially limited range of motion. To address this loss of motion, a direct
osteosynthesis technique has been developed and is gaining popularity. This technique
involves bilateral C1 lateral mass screws connected by a transverse rod, pulling the
lateral masses to the midline and allowing the fracture to heal directly without fusion to
the adjacent segments. A retrospective study of 22 patients demonstrated a 100% union
rate at 2 years with this technique.21 A concern is that this technique may result in C1-2
instability from transverse ligament disruption; however, this concern has not
manifested as a clinical problem.
Axis Fractures
The three main injury patterns of the axis are odontoid fractures, traumatic spondylolisthesis
(hangman fracture), and C2 body fractures (Resource 3).
Treatment decisions for these injuries are guided by patient age, fracture pattern, and fracture
stability.
Odontoid Fractures
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
The two subgroups of patients who sustain odontoid fractures are young patients with a high-
energy mechanism of injury and elderly patients with a low-energy mechanism of injury, such
as fall from a standing height.
Because patients are living longer, the incidence of odontoid fractures will continue to
increase.
Odontoid fractures are classified according the Anderson and D’Alonzo classification.

Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
The Anderson and D’Alonzo classification is the preferred classification system for
guiding management22 (Figure 5). A type I injury is an avulsion of the tip of the dens,
into which the alar ligaments insert. Because of the association with craniocervical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
13/40

distraction injuries, this needs to be ruled out. Type II injuries are fractures that extend
through the waist of the dens and exit above the atlantoaxial articulation. Because the
body of the dens is trabecular bone, these injuries are common in patients with
osteoporosis, in whom these injuries may be considered insufficiency fractures.23 Type
III injuries are transverse fractures that extend into the C2 body below the atlantoaxial
articulation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
14/40

Figure 5 Illustrations show the classification of odontoid fractures. (Reproduced from
Anderson PA, Hah RJ: Occipitocervical and subaxial cervical trauma, in Truumees E,
Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 395-418.)
Management
The management of type I and type III injuries usually is nonsurgical.
Management of type II injuries continues to be a subject of debate, especially in the geriatric
patient population.

Management
Because the transverse atlantal ligament is intact in patients with a type I injury, these
fractures typically are stable and can be successfully managed via immobilization in a
cervical orthosis, assuming no associated craniocervical injury is present. Type III injuries
extend below the waist of the dens and subsequently have a larger surface area of
cancellous bone and more robust blood supply than type II injuries. Therefore, type III
injuries generally can be managed via immobilization in a cervical orthosis.24 Type III
injuries can displace anteroinferiorly or shorten; therefore, close initial radiographic
monitoring is required to assess for injuries that may require surgical stabilization.
Management of type II injuries remains a subject of debate.25 Because of the low surface
area for bone healing and poor blood supply, type II injuries through the dens are at
high risk of nonunion. Additional risk factors for nonunion include 5mm or more of initial
displacement, angulation greater than 11°, a comminuted fracture pattern, posterior
displacement, and advanced age.24 Immobilization in a halo vest may be considered in
young patients who have a minimally displaced fracture without neurologic injury.26 One
caveat is that elderly patients poorly tolerate halo vest immobilization. In addition,
recent evidence suggests that for elderly patients, a cervical orthosis provides equivalent
outcomes with a lower complication rate than halo vest immobilization.27 Despite the
increasing incidence of type II odontoid fractures in elderly patients, evidence on optimal
management is conflicting.24,28,29 Some evidence suggests that a nonunion usually is

9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
15/40

well tolerated and the risk of neurologic decline is low.30,31 The authors of this lesson
believe that surgical treatment should be considered in active patients without cognitive
impairment; however, nonsurgical treatment is preferred in individuals with low
demands or cognitive impairment.
Surgical management consists of the use of an anterior odontoid screw or posterior C1-2
fusion. The benefit of using an odontoid screw is that it involves a motion-sparing
procedure. It typically is reserved for patients with an anterior-superior to posterior-
inferior fracture pattern (Figure 6) without substantial comminution, which can be
managed via closed reduction. This method allows for compression across the fracture
site with the use of one or two lag screws. The procedure leads to successful fracture
union in 90% of properly selected patients.32 Anterior bone quality within the body of C2
is poor in elderly patients, increasing their risk for screw cutout with this technique33
(Figure 7). A recent retrospective review suggested that this approach can safely be used
in the geriatric patient population but preoperative functional status is the main
predictor of perioperative complications.34
Figure 6 Sagittal CT scan of a cervical spine shows an odontoid screw and an oblique
anterior-superior to posterior-inferior fracture pattern amenable to compression with

the use of a lag screw. (Courtesy of John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
Figure 7 Lateral radiograph of a cervical spine demonstrates the typical pattern of loss
of fixation of an odontoid screw observed in elderly patients because of poor bone
quality within the C2 vertebral body. (Courtesy of John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
If a patient is unable to tolerate an anterior procedure or the fracture pattern is not
amenable to a lag screw technique, the next alternative is C1-2 posterior fusion (Figure
8). Fusion will result in loss of 50% of head rotation because the C1-2 joint will be locked
in a neutral position. Several options are available for this fusion; however, the C1 lateral
mass with a C2 pedicle screw is the most popular technique.63 Preoperative CT
angiography is important to appreciate the course of the vertebral arteries because
abnormal arterial locations may preclude safe C1 or C2 screw placement. Bone quality
for posterior screws at these levels generally is good, even in elderly patients; therefore,
this technique is preferred over anterior odontoid screws if surgical treatment is
selected in this patient population.

Figure 8 Lateral radiograph of a cervical spine with an odontoid fracture demonstrates
posterior C1-2 fusion with the use of C1 lateral mass and C2 pedicle screws. (Courtesy of
John France, MD, Morgantown, WV.)
Traumatic Spondylolisthesis of the Axis
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
The mechanism of injury in patients with traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman
fracture) most commonly is hyperextension.
The Levine classification is the most common classification system to describe these injuries.

Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
The hyperextension mechanism associated with hangman fractures leads to a traumatic
separation of the anterior and posterior elements through the C2 ring (Figure 9). Classic
descriptions of this injury pattern were limited to the bilateral pars interarticularis;
however, but injuries can include the pedicles, the posterior C2 vertebral body, and the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
18/40

lamina. In addition, the hyperextension mechanism may lead to injury of the C2-3 disk
and C2-C3 facet dislocation. The typical hangman fracture leads to expansion of the
canal, similar to a Jefferson fracture of C1 because both the anterior and posterior
portions of the ring become separated. In this situation, an associated neurologic injury
is uncommon.35 The exception is the atypical hangman fracture. In this injury pattern, a
coronal fracture occurs through the posterior C2 vertebral body at which the inner
diameter of the C2 ring is preserved. If this intact ring is substantially displaced, spinal
cord injuries can occur.
Figure 9 Parasagittal CT scan of a cervical spine shows a displaced fracture through the
pars interarticularis at C2, a typical hangman type II fracture. (Courtesy of John France,
MD, Morgantown, WV.)
The Levine and Edwards modification of the Effendi classification of traumatic
spondylolisthesis of the axis (Figure 10) currently is used. A type I injury is a
nondisplaced fracture through the posterior elements. A type IIa (Figure 11) injury is
associated with substantial angulation without translation, and the fracture line is in a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:39 AM
AAOS | Cervical Spine Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089
19/40

more horizontal plane. A type II injury is displaced and is associated with more than 3
mm of anterior translation of C2 on C3. A type III injury is associated with substantial
angulation with displacement and an associated C2-3 facet dislocation.
Figure 10 Illustrations show the classification of traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis.
(Reproduced from Anderson PA, Hah RJ: Occipitocervical and subaxial cervical trauma, in
Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 395-418.)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004089

Figure 11 Lateral radiograph of a cervical spine demonstrates the pattern of a type IIA
hangman fracture with a more horizontal fracture line through the pars interarticularis
and angulation rather than translation through the C2-3 disk space, suggesting a flexion
distraction injury that may further displace with traction. (Courtesy of John France, MD,
Morgantown, WV.)
Management
Most patients can be successfully treated via external immobilization in a halo vest or a
cervical orthosis for 6 to 12 weeks.
Surgical indications include type IIa fractures with severe angulation, type II fractures that
cannot be reduced or in which reduction cannot be maintained via external immobilization,
type III fractures with disruption of the C2-3 disk and/or a facet dislocation, and inability to
achieve or maintain fracture reduction.

Management

21/40

Type I injuries routinely can be managed via immobilization in a cervical orthosis.
Posterior surgical management via open reduction of the facets and fusion is indicated
for type III injuries. The management of type II injuries continues to be a subject of
debate;24 however, data from a recent retrospective study suggested that injuries with
less than 5 mm of initial translation and less than 15° of angulation can be successfully
managed nonsurgically.35 If surgical management is indicated, potential options include
posterior C1 through C3 fusion, C2-3 fusion with the use of pars screws at C2 and lateral
mass screws at C3, C2-3 anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion, and osteosynthesis
fixation with the use of a C2 pedicle screw.36 Anterior and posterior approaches are
reasonable methods to address these injuries,37 with C2-3 anterior cervical diskectomy
and fusion being preferred by many surgeons.
Axis Body Fractures
Axis body fractures are sagittal (type I), coronal (type II), or transverse (type III).
These injuries typically are stable and are commonly managed via immobilization in a cervical
orthosis, with the exception of displaced type III injuries. Approximately 25% of injuries
necessitate surgical management because of displacement.38
Subaxial Spine Injuries (C3 through C7)
Background, Diagnosis, and Classification
Subaxial trauma represents 65% of cervical spine fractures and 75% of cervical spine
dislocations39 (Resource 4)
Several classification systems are available, including the Cervical Spine Injury Severity Score,
the Subaxial Cervical Spine Injury Classification, and the AO Spine Subaxial Cervical Spine
Injury Classification.

The spinous process fracture may be stable or unstable and may be part of an extension or
flexion injury. An MRI may aid in defining stability by identifying associated ligamentous
disruptions.
The incidence of vertebral artery injuries is higher in patients with a subaxial cervical
transverse process fracture and in patients with a facet subluxation/dislocation or injury to
the upper cervical spine.43 CT angiography may be warranted in patients with fractures from
the occiput to C2, subaxial facet dislocations, fractures through the transverse foramen,
displaced fractures, and neurologic injury.44,45
Although vertebral artery injuries are more easily recognized, management remains
controversial.46 Some studies indicate that anticoagulation increases the risks of
complications without improving outcomes.47
Type A1: compression injuries to a single end plate
Type A2: coronal fracture through both end plates but sparing the posterior vertebral wall
Type TA1 and A2 injuries can be successfully managed with the use of a cervical orthosis.
Type A3: incomplete burst fractures involving a single end plate with extension into the
posterior wall
Type A4: complete burst fracture with involvement of both end plates and fracture extension
into the posterior wall (Figure 13, A)
Care must be taken to identify injury to the posterior osteoligamentous complex, neurologic
injury, or substantial retropulsion of the posterior body wall. In the absence of these findings,
immobilization in a cervical orthosis may be considered. In addition, type A4 injuries typically
are associated with more comminution to the anterior vertebral body and subsequently have
less resistance to settling. Therefore, nonsurgical management of these injuries is less likely
to be successful than nonsurgical management of type A3 injuries. If surgical management is
indicated, anterior corpectomy with strut grafting is recommended48 (Figure 13, B)
Secondary posterior fusion may be required if substantial disruption of the posterior
stabilizers is present.

Examples include flexion compression or teardrop injuries and burst fractures, which occur
with a flexion–axial loading mechanism of injury. A classic sagittal split in the vertebral body
that meets the coronal fracture to form a T shape can be observed on axial CT scans and is
the hallmark of a teardrop flexion compression injury.
Surgical management typically is indicated.
The approach is dictated by the degree of compromise of the anterior vertebral column
and posterior tension band disruption. The anterior approach with a corpectomy and strut
graft is most often preferred. The need for additional posterior fusion depends on the
amount of concomitant posterior tension disruption. In patients with a purely posterior
disruption without vertebral body involvement, posterior fusion would be the preferred
treatment option.
Type B3: extension injuries with anterior tension band compromise
In the mobile spine, these injuries may present as compromise to the anterior longitudinal
ligament or the anterior disk and, occasionally, may be observed in combination with a
spinous process fracture, the teardrop avulsion. Surgeons must be extremely careful using
the term teardrop because it refers to the highly unstable flexion compression injury already
mentioned and also is used by radiologists to describe this more benign avulsion injury being
discussed here. Therefore, the use of the term teardrop should be avoided, giving preference
to calling this fracture an extension-avulsion injury. Fractures in this category usually are
managed nonsurgically with the use of a hard collar.
In hyperostotic spines (ankylosing spondylitis/diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis), type
B3 injuries are highly unstable and are associated with an elevated risk of morbidity or
mortality.49-51 Surgeons must maintain high vigilance in the treatment of patients with a stiff,
hyperostotic, or ankylosed spine and assume that these injuries are unstable even if they
appear benign on initial CT scans (Figure 14).
Management typically includes reduction with posterior long-segment (three levels above
and below) fusion52 (Figure 15).
Extension injuries also may be associated with central spinal cord syndrome in elderly
patients. Some studies suggest that early decompression may facilitate neurologic
recovery;53 however, surgical indications remain a topic of debate.49,54

Type F4: facet subluxation or dislocation without fracture
More than 50% of patients with a flexion-distraction injury also have facet dislocations.59
The initial management of type F4 injuries is controversial, and treatment decisions are
guided by patient and institutional factors.
Immediate closed reduction should be performed in patients with a complete spinal cord
injury.
Two options are available for patients who are neurologically intact or have an incomplete
spinal cord injury. The first option is to obtain an MRI before attempted reduction. If disk
herniation is present, diskectomy with open anterior reduction may be considered. If no
disk herniation is present, closed reduction may be attempted. The second option is to
attempt closed reduction before obtaining an MRI in an awake patient in whom a reliable
neurologic examination can be performed; this has been demonstrated to be safe in
cooperative, awake patients. The latter option is preferred approach of the authors of this
lesson.
MRI is indicated if closed reduction is unsuccessful or if neurologic symptoms develop
during traction reduction, after successful reduction but before surgical stabilization, or in
